title: Garde à vue pour Norman et Gabriel  (In Custody for Norman and Gabriel)

segments.t: Following a chaotic birthday joyride, YouTuber Norman Thavaud is taken to the police station for speeding without his driver's license. Gabriel rushes to the station, only to find a panicked Norman desperate to abandon his dream role in Jacques Audiard's upcoming film. Listen to the scene in French first. Don't worry about catching every word.
Bonsoir. Que se passe-t-il?
M. Norman Thavaud roulait en excès de vitesse.
Le juge pourrait lui retirer le permis.
Puis-je le voir?
Par ici. Il est en cellule de dégrisement.
Tu joues à quoi? Tu ne veux plus faire le film?
Il pense déjà que je suis un loser.
Arrête, il t'a casté, tu l'as convaincu.
Il n'est pas de mon monde, pas mon univers.
Je vais me ridiculiser.
Appelle-le, annule et qu'on en finisse.
Bonjour Jacques. C'est Gabriel Sarda.
Norman ne veut pas faire votre film.
Ne haussez pas la voix!
Vous avez bu?
On m'embarque aussi?
Je suis un raté.
Pas du tout. Vous avez été casté dans un film d'Audiard.
Let's walk through the tense police station encounter step by step.
Bonsoir. Que se passe-t-il?
'Good evening. What is going on?' After dusk, 'good evening' replaces 'good day', and 'what passes itself?' inserts a '-t-' sound bridge so it is pronounced smoothly in French.
M. Norman Thavaud roulait en excès de vitesse.
'Mr. Norman Thavaud was speeding.' Literally 'rolling in excess of speed', that official police expression is how French law describes speeding.
Le juge pourrait lui retirer le permis.
'The judge could take away his license.' Rather than saying 'his license', French says 'to-him withdraw the license', pairing 'the' with an indirect recipient.
Puis-je le voir?
'May I see him?' When 'can' flips ahead of 'I' in polite questions, it switches to a special formal shape that means 'may I' in French.
Par ici. Il est en cellule de dégrisement.
'This way. He is in the sobering-up cell.' Guiding someone down a hall takes 'by here' for 'this way', while 'un-tipsying cell' is police terminology for the drunk tank in French.
Tu joues à quoi? Tu ne veux plus faire le film?
'What are you playing at? You don't want to do the film anymore?' Literally 'you play at what?', putting 'at what' at the end makes Gabriel's question sound sharp in French.
Il pense déjà que je suis un loser.
'He already thinks that I am a loser.' Everyday youth slang borrows 'loser' straight from English, keeping 'already' right after 'thinks' in French.
Arrête, il t'a casté, tu l'as convaincu.
'Stop it, he cast you, you convinced him.' Film insiders turn English 'cast' into a French action with an '-e' past ending, paired with a cognate of 'convinced'.
Il n'est pas de mon monde, pas mon univers.
'He is not from my world, not my universe.' Saying someone is 'of my world' covers 'from my world', closing with the cognate 'universe' minus its final '-e' in French.
Je vais me ridiculiser.
'I am going to make a fool of myself.' Packing all of 'make a fool of myself' into a single reflexive action built on 'ridicule' is classic compact French.
Appelle-le, annule et qu'on en finisse.
'Call him, cancel and let's get it over with.' Closing with 'that one of-it finishes!' is a vivid, impatient idiom you'll hear for 'let's get it over with!'.
Bonjour Jacques. C'est Gabriel Sarda.
'Hello Jacques. It is Gabriel Sarda.' Even on a pretend late-night call, Gabriel identifies himself with 'it is' plus his first name and surname in French.
Norman ne veut pas faire votre film.
'Norman does not want to do your movie.' Addressing the revered director calls for polite 'your' before 'film', right after 'wants not to make' in French.
Ne haussez pas la voix!
'Do not raise your voice!' Built from the root meaning 'high', the command means 'raise', and French uses 'the voice' rather than 'your voice'.
Vous avez bu?
'Have you been drinking?' Just three short words—literally 'you have drunk?'—cover both 'did you drink?' and 'have you been drinking?' in French.
On m'embarque aussi?
'Are you locking me up too?' Literally 'one embarks me too?', nautical 'embark' doubles as colloquial slang for hauling someone into custody in French.
Je suis un raté.
'I am a failure.' Turning 'missed' or 'botched' into a label for a person gives you a blunt, self-pitying term that means 'a failure' in French.
Pas du tout. Vous avez été casté dans un film d'Audiard.

'Not at all. You were cast in an Audiard movie.' Echoing formal 'you have been cast' gives Gabriel's reminder the weight of an official honor in French. Now let's listen to the whole scene again at normal speed, and see how much more you catch.
Bonsoir. Que se passe-t-il?
M. Norman Thavaud roulait en excès de vitesse.
Le juge pourrait lui retirer le permis.
Puis-je le voir?
Par ici. Il est en cellule de dégrisement.
Tu joues à quoi? Tu ne veux plus faire le film?
Il pense déjà que je suis un loser.
Arrête, il t'a casté, tu l'as convaincu.
Il n'est pas de mon monde, pas mon univers.
Je vais me ridiculiser.
Appelle-le, annule et qu'on en finisse.
Bonjour Jacques. C'est Gabriel Sarda.
Norman ne veut pas faire votre film.
Ne haussez pas la voix!
Vous avez bu?
On m'embarque aussi?
Je suis un raté.
Pas du tout. Vous avez été casté dans un film d'Audiard.
After feigning a cancellation call to Audiard and clashing with the police officer, Gabriel finds himself locked inside the drunk tank alongside his anxious client. See you next time!
Bonne journée!
